newsitem.title: USA: US disappointed with results of Canada trip to Cuba.
newsitem.headline: US disappointed with results of Canada trip to Cuba.

text.p: The United States was disapointed with the results of Canadian foreign minister Lloyd Axworthy's recent trip to Cuba, a senior Clinton administration official said on Monday.
Axworthy was the top Canadian official to visit the Communist-ruled island in two decades when he went to Havana in January for talks with Cuban President Fidel Castro and other officials.

"We appreciate the efforts of the Canadian government to try to promote democracy and human rights, and we know that it was in that spirit that the foreign minister went to Cuba," Commerce Undersecretary Stuart Eizenstat said.

"We were disappointed with the results," added Eizenstat, who is also Clinton's special envoy for Cuban affairs, during a conference on the so-called Helms-Burton law hosted by U.S., Canadian and European think tanks.
Despite being close allies and trading partners, Ottawa and Washington differ sharply on their policies toward Cuba.
The United States has kept an embargo against Cuba for over 35 years while Canada has good relations with Castro's government and is a major investor in the island.
They also are at odds over the Helms-Burton law, a U.S. legislation that penalizes foreign companies doing business with properties confiscated from Americans in Cuba.
Eizenstat noted that only two of some 14 points in a joint declaration Axworthy signed in Cuba dealt with human rights.
One referred to the creation of a "complaints office" within Cuba's parliament for citizens to voice grievances.

"We had hoped that there would be an ombudsman office, separate from the government ... that would have provided a forum for Cuban citizens to register complaints about deprivations of human rights," Eizenstat said.

"Instead, they have a complaints office that could be complaints that your electricity is not working, and, rather than being at arm's length, it's in the National Assembly, which is a thoroughly government-controlled or Communist-dominated institution," he added.
The United States was also dismayed by the fact that the communique seemed to favor only Canadian nongovernmental organizations operating in the island.

"So, one has to say, for the first visit of a Canadian foreign minister (to Cuba) in 37 years, we would have hoped for more," added Eizenstat, who nevertheless said Washington knew that Ottawa had made a sincere effort.
Canadian officials have defended their policy towards Cuba pointing out that U.S. sanctions have failed to weaken Castro, who has been in power since 1959.
